description: What this shows: Operational health of an XRPL node: sync state, ledger progress, caches, storage, job queue, and network economy.  —  Use it to: Get an at-a-glance read on whether the node is healthy, synced, and keeping up with the network.

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*A single at-a-glance verdict: is this node healthy and doing its job (fully synced and keeping up with the network)?*

###### How it's computed:
*1 (Healthy) only when server_state == Full AND the validated ledger age is under 30s; otherwise 0 (Not Healthy). Combines server_info{metric="server_state"} and ledgermaster_validated_ledger_age.*

###### Reading it:
*Green "Healthy" = full sync and current. Red "Not Healthy" = not full, or lagging the network (catching up, flapping, or stalled).*

###### Healthy range:
*Healthy (green) in steady state.*

###### Watch for:
*Any sustained Not Healthy — drill into the Operating Mode and Validated Ledger Age panels below to see whether it is a state or a lag problem.*

###### Keywords:
- **Full** *(per node)* — the node has the current validated ledger and complete recent history.
- **Validated ledger age** *(per node)* — seconds since the last freshly validated ledger.

###### Computation boundary:
*Result: Per node — a boolean AND of two native metrics.*
*Recorded in xrpld code as native metrics (beast::insight); the collector only forwards them; the Grafana query combines them.*

###### Source:
[app/misc/NetworkOPs.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/xrpld/app/misc/NetworkOPs.cpp)

###### Function:
`NetworkOPsImp::setMode / getValidatedLedgerAge`

[Server states](https://xrpl.org/docs/concepts/networks-and-servers/rippled-server-states) · [Telemetry glossary](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/docs/telemetry-glossary.md)

panels.title: Node Health [$xrpl_network_type]

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*How old the most recently validated ledger is, in seconds.*

###### How it's computed:
*Current value of the validated-ledger-age gauge, refreshed each collection interval.*

###### Reading it:
*Lower is better; it should stay near the network close interval.*

###### Healthy range:
*Under about 7 seconds on a healthy node.*

###### Watch for:
*Values above 20 seconds mean the node is falling behind the network.*

###### Keywords:
- **Validated ledger** *(network-wide)* — a ledger confirmed final by the trusted validator quorum; its contents never change.
- **Ledger close interval** *(network-wide)* — the network's steady ledger rhythm — roughly one closed ledger every 3-5 seconds on Mainnet.

###### Computation boundary:
*Result: Per node — each series is one server's own value.*
*Recorded in xrpld code as a native metric (beast::insight); the collector only forwards it; the Grafana query selects and aggregates it.*

###### Source:
[LedgerMaster.h](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/xrpld/app/ledger/LedgerMaster.h)

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*How often the node requests a ledger from its peers.*

###### How it's computed:
*Per-second rate of ledger-fetch requests over a 5-minute window.*

###### Reading it:
*Near zero in steady state; elevated while catching up.*

###### Healthy range:
*Close to zero once fully synced.*

###### Watch for:
*A sustained high rate means the node is repeatedly missing ledgers and back-filling from peers.*

###### Keywords:
- **Ledger acquire (inbound fetch)** *(per node)* — fetching a specific missing ledger from peers; tracked by duration and outcome (complete/failed).
- **Back-fill / catch-up** *(per node)* — fetching missing historical ledgers from peers to fill gaps or reach the network tip.

###### Computation boundary:
*Result: Per node — each series is one server's own value.*
*Recorded in xrpld code as a native metric (beast::insight); the collector only forwards it; the Grafana query selects and aggregates it.*

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Rate at which a locally built ledger hash fails to match the network-validated hash.*

###### How it's computed:
*Per-second rate of history-mismatch events over a 5-minute window.*

###### Reading it:
*Flat at zero is the only healthy reading.*

###### Healthy range:
*Zero.*

###### Watch for:
*Any nonzero value indicates consensus divergence or database corruption and warrants immediate investigation.*

###### Keywords:
- **Ledger history mismatch** *(per node)* — when a locally built ledger's hash does not match the network-validated hash.
- **Validated ledger** *(network-wide)* — a ledger confirmed final by the trusted validator quorum; its contents never change.
- **Consensus** *(network event)* — the protocol by which validators agree on the next ledger's transaction set and close time.

###### Computation boundary:
*Result: Per node — each series is one server's own value.*
*Computed in xrpld code (MetricsRegistry, OpenTelemetry SDK) and exported as a metric; the collector only forwards it; the Grafana query selects and aggregates it.*

###### Source:

###### What this is:
*The lag between published and validated ledger ages, in seconds.*

###### How it's computed:
*Published ledger age minus validated ledger age, as a single derived value.*

###### Reading it:
*Near zero is healthy; a positive value is how far publishing trails validation.*

###### Healthy range:
*Close to zero.*

###### Watch for:
*A growing gap means the publish pipeline is falling behind and subscribers may see stale data.*

###### Keywords:
- **Validated ledger** *(network-wide)* — a ledger confirmed final by the trusted validator quorum; its contents never change.
- **Published ledger** *(per node)* — the most recent validated ledger the node has finished publishing to its subscribers.

###### Computation boundary:

*Recorded in xrpld code as a native metric (beast::insight); the collector only forwards it; the Grafana query selects and aggregates it.*

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Latency of the I/O service loop, at the 95th percentile in milliseconds.*

###### How it's computed:
*I/O loop latency samples aggregated to their 95th percentile per node over a 5-minute window.*

###### Reading it:
*Lower is better; it reflects how promptly queued I/O work runs.*

###### Healthy range:
*A few milliseconds; brief spikes are tolerable.*

###### Watch for:
*Sustained values above a few hundred ms indicate thread-pool saturation or blocking operations.*

###### Keywords:
- **I/O scheduler** *(per node)* — the queue that serializes NodeStore disk reads and writes.
- **NodeStore** *(per node)* — the key-value object store holding ledger data (tree nodes), backed by NuDB.

###### Computation boundary:
*Result: Per node — each series is one server's own value.*
*Recorded in xrpld code as a native metric (beast::insight); the collector only forwards it; the Grafana query selects and aggregates it.*

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*The share of recent wall-clock time the node spent in Full mode.*

###### How it's computed:
*Per-second rate of the Full-mode duration counter divided by the sum of the per-second rates of all five mode duration counters.*

###### Reading it:
*Higher is better; 1.0 means the node was fully synced for the entire window.*

###### Healthy range:
*At or above 0.99.*

###### Watch for:
*Values dropping below 0.9, meaning the node spent meaningful time outside Full mode.*

###### Keywords:
- **Operating mode / server state** *(per node)* — the node's sync level: Disconnected, Connected, Syncing, Tracking, Full (and Validating/Proposing).

###### Computation boundary:
*Result: Per node — each series is one server's own value.*
*Recorded in xrpld code as a native metric (beast::insight); the collector only forwards it; the Grafana query selects and aggregates it.*

panels.title: % Time in Full [$xrpl_network_type]

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Fraction of recent wall-clock time the node spent in each operating mode (Disconnected, Connected, Syncing, Tracking, Full).*

###### How it's computed:
*Per-second rate of each per-mode duration counter divided by the sum of all five mode rates, giving each mode's time share.*

###### Reading it:
*The Full share should sit at or near 1.0 and dominate; other shares should be near 0.*

###### Healthy range:
*Full share close to 1.0.*

###### Watch for:
*Share accumulating in Syncing, Connected, or Disconnected means the node is not staying fully synced.*

###### Keywords:
- **Operating mode / server state** *(per node)* — the node's sync level: Disconnected, Connected, Syncing, Tracking, Full (and Validating/Proposing).

###### Computation boundary:
*Result: Per node — each series is one server's own value.*
*Recorded in xrpld code as a native metric (beast::insight); the collector only forwards it; the Grafana query selects and aggregates it.*

panels.title: Operating Mode (Time Share)

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Transitions into each operating mode, per interval.*

###### How it's computed:
*round(increase(...[$__interval])) over each per-mode transition counter. $__interval tiles the buckets exactly, so each bar is the transitions in that bucket and the legend Total is the true count; $__rate_interval would overlap each bucket by one scrape and inflate it (measured +5% at a 36h range, +26% zoomed in). round() removes increase()'s extrapolation, which otherwise reports fractional counts. The series stays correct across an xrpld restart (the counters reset to 0).*

###### Reading it:
*Zero is healthy; each bar is the mode changes within that bucket. Brief flaps show up here even when they are too short to appear on Operating Mode (State Timeline), which can only sample state once per scrape.*

###### Healthy range:
*Few transitions once the node is stable in Full mode.*

###### Watch for:
*Frequent transitions out of Full, or into Disconnected or Syncing, indicate instability.*

###### Keywords:
- **Operating mode / server state** *(per node)* — the node's sync level: Disconnected, Connected, Syncing, Tracking, Full (and Validating/Proposing).

###### Computation boundary:
*Result: Per node — each series is one server's own value.*
*Recorded in xrpld code as a native metric (beast::insight); the collector only forwards it; the Grafana query selects and aggregates it.*

panels.title: Operating Mode Transitions

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Which operating mode the node is accumulating time in right now, one line per state, normalized to seconds per second.*

###### How it's computed:
*Per-second rate of each state's duration counter, scaled from microseconds to seconds. The five lines sum to about 1.0 because the node is always in exactly one state.*

###### Reading it:
*The line sitting near 1.0 is the state the node is currently in; the others sit at 0. A handover between two lines marks a state change, and its width is how long that state lasted.*

###### Healthy range:
*Full near 1.0 with every other line at 0.*

###### Watch for:
*Time accumulating in Connected or Syncing means the node is catching up rather than serving; repeated handovers mean it is flapping.*

###### Keywords:
- **Operating mode / server state** *(per node)* — the node's sync level: Disconnected, Connected, Syncing, Tracking, Full.

panels.title: NodeStore Throughput

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Fraction of object-store reads that returned an object. `node_reads_hit` counts fetches that found the object whatever served them, so this is not a cache-hit rate.*

###### How it's computed:
*Per-second rate of `node_reads_hit` divided by the per-second rate of `node_reads_total`, as a single ratio per node.*

###### Reading it:
*A value near 1.0 means almost every read finds its object; dips mean reads are missing.*

###### Healthy range:
*Close to 1.0 on a node that holds the data it is being asked for.*

###### Watch for:
*A sustained drop means the node is repeatedly asked for objects it does not have, which usually accompanies backfill or a gap in history.*

###### Keywords:
- **NodeStore** *(per node)* — the key-value object store holding ledger data (tree nodes), backed by NuDB.

###### Computation boundary:
*Result: Per node — each series is one server's own value.*
*Computed in xrpld code (MetricsRegistry, OpenTelemetry SDK) and exported as a metric; the collector only forwards it; the Grafana query selects and aggregates it.*

panels.title: FullBelowCache Hit Rate [$xrpl_network_type]

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Which sync state each node is in right now: Disconnected, Connected, Syncing, Tracking or Full. Only a Full node holds the current validated ledger and can answer authoritatively.*

###### How it's computed:
*The `server_state` gauge, the node's operating mode as an integer 0-4, value-mapped to a name and colour: 0 Disconnected (red), 1 Connected (yellow), 2 Syncing (orange), 3 Tracking (blue), 4 Full (green). No rate or aggregation — it is the instantaneous state.*

###### Reading it:
*One tile per node. Green FULL is the steady state; any other colour says the node is not yet serving the current ledger and how far along it is.*

###### Healthy range:
*FULL on every node.*

###### Watch for:
*A node leaving FULL and staying out, or flapping between TRACKING and FULL — that points at ledger acquisition falling behind rather than a connectivity fault. Cross-check Operating Mode (Time Share) and Validated Ledger Age.*

###### Keywords:
- **Operating mode / server state** *(per node)* — the node's sync level: Disconnected, Connected, Syncing, Tracking, Full (and Validating/Proposing).

###### Computation boundary:
*Result: Per node — each series is one server's own value.*

panels.description:
###### What this is:
*Time to fetch a missing ledger from peers, at the 95th percentile, with a separate line per acquisition outcome.*

###### How it's computed:
*Per-acquire durations aggregated to their 95th percentile per node over a 5-minute window, grouped by outcome, so complete, failed and aborted acquisitions are never mixed into one percentile.*

###### Reading it:
*Read the Complete line as the real fetch latency; lower is better, and it is populated mainly during sync or back-fill. Aborted means the acquisition was abandoned before it finished, so its span also covers the idle time it spent waiting to be reaped (at least a minute when swept, or any age when a shutdown or an admin fetch_info clear drops it) and is not comparable to a fetch time.*

###### Healthy range:
*Complete is low when synced, and higher and more active while catching up. Failed and Aborted are normally absent.*

###### Watch for:
*A spike in Complete signals the node is falling behind or recovering from a fork. A persistent Aborted line means acquisitions are routinely abandoned before they finish, so its height reflects how long they sat unfinished, not how slow the network is.*

###### Keywords:
- **Ledger acquire (inbound fetch)** *(per node)* — fetching a specific missing ledger from peers; tracked by duration and outcome — complete, failed (gave up after its retry limit, or hit unusable ledger data), or aborted (abandoned before finishing).
- **Back-fill / catch-up** *(per node)* — fetching missing historical ledgers from peers to fill gaps or reach the network tip.
- **Fork** *(network-wide)* — when nodes validate divergent ledger chains instead of a single agreed history.

###### Computation boundary:

Job Queue Saturation (Running vs Limit)
panels.description:
###### What this is:
*How close each concurrency-capped job type is to its ceiling. JobQueue enforces a per-type limit on how many jobs of that type may run at once, and the tight ones carry ledger-sync traffic: makeFetchPack 1, ledgerRequest 3, ledgerData 3, updatePaths 1, fetchTxnData 5. A type at its ceiling cannot start more work no matter how many workers are idle, so this is a different kind of limit from CPU or disk.*

###### How it's computed:
*Each jobq_<jobtype>_running gauge divided by that type's own limit from JobTypes.h, so every line shares one 0-to-1 axis. 1.0 means running equals the limit. Multiply a reading by the limit shown in its legend to recover the raw job count. JobQueue::collect snapshots all three per-type counters under the queue's own lock and publishes them after releasing it, on the 1-second export cycle.*

###### Reading it:
*Read the distance to 1.0, not the absolute height. Below 1.0 the type has spare slots and its queue wait is not the limit's fault. Touching 1.0 briefly is normal work. Sitting at 1.0 means the type is pinned at its ceiling and every further job of that type is being deferred rather than started, which is what turns into queue wait downstream. Because the limits differ, a raw count of 3 is saturation for ledgerRequest but only 60 percent for fetchTxnData; normalizing is what makes the lines comparable.*

###### Healthy range:
*Below 1.0, with brief touches under load.*

###### Watch for:
*A line flat at 1.0: that type is the binding constraint. ledgerRequest pinned means the 3 slots shared by RcvGetLedger and RcvGetObjByHash are full, so peer ledger and object requests are queueing behind each other; the Ledger Data and Sync dashboard splits that wait by handler and shows the matching deferred depth. ledgerData or fetchTxnData pinned means inbound ledger data cannot be absorbed and validated ledger age will grow. makeFetchPack or updatePaths pinned at their limit of 1 means a single long job is blocking the whole type. These are sampled gauges, so a line that never reaches 1.0 is not proof the type was never momentarily saturated.*

###### Keywords:
- **Job queue / job type** *(per node)* — xrpld's worker-thread pool; every unit of background work is enqueued under a named job type.
- **Concurrency limit** *(per node)* — the cap on how many jobs of one type may run at once; a type at its cap cannot start more work.
- **Deferred job** *(per node)* — a job held back because its type is already at its concurrency limit; the leading indicator of queue backpressure.

###### Computation boundary:
*Result: Per node — each series is one server's own value.*
*Recorded in xrpld code as a native metric (beast::insight); the collector only forwards it; the Grafana query selects and aggregates it.*

[core/JobQueue.cpp](https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/blob/develop/src/libxrpl/core/detail/JobQueue.cpp)
